meta.summary: 32 sets · 4 Parts × 8 question formats · 640 questions · scripts ready for ElevenLabs

bullets.lead: Every script rewritten to IELTS standard.
bullets.text: Answers now come in question order, questions paraphrase the audio rather than copying it, and each set contains real distractors (corrections, changed plans, “used to be X, now Y”, options mentioned then rejected) instead of one-line question-and-answer echoes.

In the previous edition many sets (e.g. P1-MA 11-20, P1-TC, P2-TC, P2-SM, P3-MA, P3-TC, P3-SM, P4-MA, P4-TC, P4-SM) asked about details that were never spoken or keyed answers that contradicted the audio. Every answer in this edition was machine-checked against the script: each is backed by a quoted evidence phrase, located in order.

bullets.lead: Map / plan sets are now real labelling tasks.
bullets.text: Letters are placed on a written layout and the speaker gives directions, so answers are no longer simply A, B, C … J in sequence.

bullets.lead: Currency and spelling match the accent
bullets.text: (pounds/pence for British sets, dollars for American, Australian and Canadian sets).

Almost every turn now carries a v4 direction tag describing how the line is said (e.g. [a little amused, disagreeing], [correcting herself, a little flustered], [relieved]), plus non-verbal cues ([chuckles], [sighs], [light laugh]), hesitations and fillers (“um”, “er”, “hmm”), and self-corrections. Very short follow-up questions are deliberately left untagged so the delivery does not sound over-acted. All tags describe something audible; visual actions were removed, as ElevenLabs advises.

bullets.lead: Answer keys follow IELTS word limits.
bullets.text: Every completion answer fits the set’s word limit, uses the word form actually spoken in the recording, and names that are not everyday words are spelled out in the audio.

For all 640 questions, each key is tied to the exact phrase in the script that gives the answer; a script confirms every phrase exists and that the phrases occur in the same order as the questions (as in the real test).
Every completion answer was checked against its word limit and against the words heard near that phrase.
Every multiple-choice, matching and map answer was reviewed by hand, option text beside the audio that supports it. Map/plan letters are shuffled so answers do not run A, B, C… in order.

sections.heading: What to know before using it

bullets.lead: IELTS / Cambridge format, not official material.
bullets.text: The sets follow the conventions of Cambridge IELTS practice tests (four parts, question types, word limits, answers in order, paraphrase and distractors). The band levels shown are estimates for practice; they have not been calibrated on real candidates, and no third-party question bank can be “Cambridge graded”.
A real IELTS part has 10 questions. Each set here is a double-length practice set by design; split it at Question 10 if you want test-length sections.

bullets.lead: Map and plan sets need drawings.
bullets.text: The written layouts stand in for the printed plans; draw each plan with the letters in the positions described before giving it to students.
Paper checks cannot catch a mispronounced answer word or a tag the model reads aloud. Generate, listen once against the answer key, and regenerate any single line that is off.

productionGuide.guidance: eleven_v4 for all 32 sets (highest quality; not the Turbo variant, which is built for live agents). Parts 1 and 3: use Text to Dialogue and assign one voice per speaker label. Parts 2 and 4: use Text to Speech with one voice.

v4 exposes only Stability and Similarity (no Style or Speed sliders, no SSML). Recommended: Stability ≈ 0.50 for dialogues (natural variation between turns), ≈ 0.60 for lectures and announcements (steadier delivery); Similarity ≈ 0.75.

Choose Voice Library voices whose own language/accent matches the set’s locale (en-GB, en-US, en-AU, en-CA). v4 keeps the accent of a voice when generating in the same language, so the voice choice sets the accent. Give each speaker in a dialogue a clearly different voice (gender, age or timbre) so candidates can tell them apart.

Square brackets carry natural-language directions such as [calm, welcoming, soft voice] or [correcting herself], and non-verbal cues such as [light laugh], [sighs], [short pause]. They are not spoken. Paste the script exactly as printed, tags included.

Scene cues (e.g. [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open], [quiet library room tone]) appear only at the start of a scene. v4 can render them, but a tag can occasionally be read as speech direction instead: if a cue misfires, delete it and layer a separately generated sound effect in your editor. Keep ambience low; IELTS audio must stay clean.

SSML <break> tags are not supported in v4. Pauses use [short pause], ellipses (…) and sentence breaks. The 30-second reading pauses between sections of a real test are added in post-production, not in the script.

All answer-bearing numbers are written as words the way a speaker says them (“oh-seven-eight-four-five… double three one”, “a hundred and forty pounds”), so v4 does not guess a reading. Spelled names are written letter by letter with ellipses (“B… R… A… N…”) to force clear, separated letters.

Where a foreign or unusual name must be said correctly, the script uses v4’s IPA syntax: the IPA in forward slashes inside double quotes, e.g. Nicéphore "/niˈɛps/". Test these once with your chosen voice; if a voice misreads one, replace it with a phonetic respelling.

Each set shows its character count. Scripts longer than about 4,500 characters are split at a speaker-turn boundary and marked with purple “Chunk 1 of 2” lines (only P1-FN in this edition): generate chunk by chunk and pass the neighbouring chunk text as previous_text / next_text (API) so tone and pacing stay continuous across the join.

Listen for: every answer word clearly audible; distractor corrections sound like natural self-corrections; no tag read aloud; letters in spelled words separated; speakers distinguishable. Regenerate a single line rather than the whole script when one turn is off.

transcript.text: Yep, we're open seven days a week. We only close on public holidays.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: What do I need to bring on my first visit? Do I need a doctor's note or anything like that?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: No doctor's note. You just fill in a short health form here. Bring photo ID though, so we can set up your membership card.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is there a minimum contract?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Our shortest contract is three months. We used to ask for six, but not anymore. After three months, it's month-to-month.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And if I had to leave before the three months were up?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Then you just pay one month's fee as a cancellation charge.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: There's no deposit or anything to lose.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That's fair.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Which classes are the busiest?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: A friend told me spin fills up.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: On most evenings, it's actually yoga, but on Monday evenings, spin is always the most popular.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Everyone's making up for the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I know the feeling.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Where are the lockers?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: The changing rooms are down in the basement, but the lockers are on the ground floor, right next to reception.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is the pool heated? I know it's premium only, but I might upgrade later.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: It is. We used to keep it at 26° Celsius, but people said it was too cold, so now it's 28.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is personal training included for new members at all?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Every new member gets one free session with a trainer. After that, it's paid.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: How do most people pay?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Most people pay monthly by card, but if you pay for the whole year by bank transfer, you get a better rate.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: We don't take cash for memberships.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Good to know.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: What time do the last classes finish?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: The last class starts at 8:00 and finishes at 9:00 p.m. The gym itself stays open until 10:00.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is there anything I need to know about the sauna?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: You don't need to book, and towels are provided. We just ask everyone to shower before going in.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And guest passes? Do I get any?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Not with standard, I'm afraid. Off-peak members get one a year, and premium members get four.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: A couple more things.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is parking on the street?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: Street parking is tricky around here, but we have our own parking lot behind the building, and it's free for members.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: My son is 15. Could he use the gym on his own?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: He can come in with you, but members need to be 16 to use the gym without supervision.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And that reduced joining fee, how long does it last?

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: That offer ends at the end of this month. Next month, it goes back up to 50.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Then I'd better come in this week.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Thanks so much, Jake.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: You're welcome, Priya.

transcript.speaker: Jake
transcript.text: See you soon.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [mock-exasperated sigh] Fair enough, I'll take registration. What about handing out the gloves and bags?

script.speaker: Sam

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [thoughtful] Then there's contacting the council about the skip collection.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [weary groan] I started on that, but it's turned into loads of phone calls. Can we share it?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [sympathetic] Sure, we'll do that one together.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [hopeful] Photos for the social media page... you're the one with the good camera.

script.speaker: Priya

script.speaker: Sam

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [approving] Good. The corporate volunteers from the bank?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [wry] They want photos for their newsletter, so send them to the pier. It's the most visible spot.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [chuckles] And the family group with the little ones?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [thinking it through] The café strip. It's flat, and it's right next to the toilets.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The scout troop?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [considering] Hmm, the rock pools will be under water at that time of day, so... [decisive] the car park. It needs a proper clear-out, and the scouts love a challenge.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [satisfied] That leaves North Beach for the regular volunteers. They know how to handle glass safely.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [enthusiastic] Perfect.

script.speaker: Sam

script.speaker: Priya

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [casual] Yep, they've said yes again.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Water bottles?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [laughs] I've got about fifty in my garage left over from the fun run. We'll use those.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [relieved] Great. And the recycling bins will come from the council depot. They confirmed that this morning.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [moving on] Now timing. Should registration open at nine?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [knowing] People always turn up early, so let's open registration at half past eight.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [agreeable] Okay. Then the clean-up itself starts at nine.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Yes. And a break at half past ten?

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [thinking, doubtful] That's only an hour and a half in. Let's make it a quarter past eleven.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [conceding] Fine, the break's at quarter past eleven. Then photos and the final count at twelve.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: And we finish at half past one?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [confirming, cheerful] That's right. The clean-up ends at one thirty, and everyone can go and enjoy the rest of the day.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: [cheerful, upbeat] Sounds like a plan. See you Saturday!

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: I'll take that one. I'm better with names and the sign-in sheet.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Okay, so Priya's on registration. I'll hand out the gloves and bags at the start.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Sounds good. What about contacting the council? Someone still needs to confirm the skip collection.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Let's both do that together actually, since it involves a few calls.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Agreed. We'll split that between us.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Who's taking photos for social media?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'll do that. I've got a decent camera on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Great. And the final count of rubbish collected at the end?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I think you should do that one, Priya, since you'll already have the clipboard.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Fine by me. Now, let's think about which group goes where.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: The under-16s group, where should they go?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'd put them in the dunes. It's safer and there's less glass.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Good thinking. What about the corporate volunteers from the bank?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Let's send them to the pier area. More visible, good for their group photos, too.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: The family group with the younger kids?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: The café strip makes sense for them. It's flat and close to the toilets.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: And the teenagers from the sixth form?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'd say the car park. It needs a proper clear out and they've got the energy for it.

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Fair enough. That leaves North Beach for the regular volunteers then.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Exactly. Now, about the benefits we should mention when we thank everyone afterwards. Composting reduces landfill, doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: Sam
transcript.text: Yes, that's the main benefit of the composting bins we're setting up.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And the car-sharing scheme people used to get here?

transcript.text: That's mainly about reducing emissions from all the extra traffic.

transcript.text: The bring-your-own-bag scheme some of the shops are running?

transcript.text: Great. I think we've covered everything.

script.text: [hopeful] Is there a café up there? That's where I'm meeting my friend.

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: [enthusiastic] There is. It's on the north balcony, overlooking the atrium, so you can look down at the fountain.

script.speaker: Visitor
script.text: [delighted] Lovely. And toilets?

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: Just behind the café, at the far north end.

script.speaker: Visitor

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: [reassuring] The lifts are at the south end, on the east side.

script.speaker: Visitor
script.text: And what's next to them, on the west side?

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: [chatty] That's the photo studio. They do passport photos, if you ever need them.

script.speaker: Visitor
script.text: [grateful, relieved] Thank you so much. That's really clear now.

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: [warm] No problem at all. Enjoy your day!

script.text: [relieved] Tuesday's fine. How long is each session? Receptionist: They're two hours each, from seven until nine.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And how many weeks does it run for? Receptionist: [careful to distinguish] The intermediate course is twelve weeks, but the beginners' one is shorter. It's eight weeks.

script.speaker: Daniel

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [curious] Where are the classes held? In the hall? Receptionist: [light laugh] No, the hall's for exercise classes. Cookery's in our training kitchen on the first floor.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Do I need to bring any equipment? Receptionist: [easy-going] Knives, pans and so on are all provided. Just bring your own apron, please.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [uncertain] What about food? Do I bring that? Receptionist: [reassuring] No, we supply all the ingredients. That's included in the fee.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Oh, that's easy. What do you start with? Receptionist: [enthusiastic] The first week is all about basic knife skills. [playful] Chopping onions without crying, that sort of thing.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [laughs] I definitely need that. Receptionist: [warm] And everyone gets a recipe booklet on the first evening, so you can practise at home.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [curious] What happens in the last week? Receptionist: [delighted] The last week's the fun one. You each cook a dinner for friends or family, and they come in and eat it.

script.speaker: Daniel

script.speaker: Daniel

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone? Receptionist: [apologetic sigh] Our card machine's being replaced at the moment, so it'll have to be by bank transfer.

script.text: [easy] That's fine. Is there anything else I should know? Receptionist: [serious, careful] Yes. If you've got any allergies, you need to tell us in advance, so Rosa can plan around them.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [cheerful] No allergies, luckily. Is there parking? Receptionist: [helpful] The front car park is pay-and-display, but the rear car park is free in the evenings.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good. And can I take the food home? Receptionist: [chuckling] You can. Most people bring a plastic container. Glass ones have been broken in the past.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [hesitant] What if I start and it's not for me? Receptionist: [kind] If you cancel during the first week, you get a full refund. After that, I'm afraid there's no refund.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [understanding] That's fair. When does the next course start? Receptionist: [thinking briefly] The August course is full, so the next one starts in September.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] September, great. And if I enjoy it, can I go on to the intermediate course? Receptionist: [encouraging] Of course. That one's always popular, so you'd need to join the waiting list.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thoughtful] I'll think about it. Thanks for your help. Receptionist: [cheerful] You're welcome. We look forward to seeing you!

script.text: [phone ringing, then answered] [organised, slightly stressed] Hello, is that Swift Movers? I'd like a quote for moving house, please.

script.speaker: Swift
script.text: It includes up to twenty boxes. Anything more is extra.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: And how much notice do you need?

script.speaker: Swift
script.text: [matter-of-fact] At least two weeks. In summer it's more like a month, but two weeks is fine at the moment.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [cautious] Is there anything that would make it more expensive?

script.speaker: Swift
script.text: [blunt] Stairs. If there are stairs at either end, we charge extra for that.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [sighs] We're on the second floor. [polite, ending the call] Okay, thanks, I'll let you know.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [hopeful] Hi, I'd like a quote for a three-bedroom move, please. It's a short distance.

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [quick, confident] Sure. That would be five hundred pounds.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [taken aback] Oh, that's more than the other company.

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [confident, persuasive] It is, but it includes our full packing service. We pack everything for you the day before.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [interested, relieved] That would save me a lot of time. How much notice do you need?

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [breezy] Just forty-eight hours, if we've got a van free.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: And is there any extra charge I should know about?

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: Only for a piano. Do you have one?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [light laugh, a bit embarrassed] Unfortunately, yes.

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [cheerful] Then there's an extra eighty pounds. [short pause] Would you like to book?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [decisive] Yes, let's do it. We'd like to move on a Wednesday if possible.

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [keyboard clicks] [thinking briefly] Wednesday the twelfth is free. The team would arrive at eight a.m. [playful] Not seven, like some companies. We give people time for breakfast.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [laughs] Eight's good. How many people will come?

script.speaker: CityMove

script.speaker: Helen

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [reassuring] You're covered for up to ten thousand pounds of damage.

script.speaker: Helen

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [proud] Yes, everything's wrapped in blankets. We stopped using bubble wrap to cut down on plastic.

script.speaker: Helen

script.speaker: CityMove

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [cautious] What if I need to cancel?

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [clear, serious] There's a fifty-pound cancellation fee if you cancel with less than fourteen days' notice.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [thoughtful] Okay. Is there anything I need to organise?

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [helpful] Yes. You'll need a parking permit for the van outside your new flat. You get that from the council.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [slightly overwhelmed] Right, I'll call them. Anything else?

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: We'll need a list of any large items, like wardrobes or the piano, so we can plan the loading.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [efficient] I'll email one over. Is there a reference number?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [reading back] C, M, two seven four.

script.speaker: CityMove
script.text: [warm] That's it. And we'll call you on the Monday before the move to confirm everything.

script.speaker: Helen

script.speaker: CityMove

script.text: [laid-back] Hi, Kate. I'd like to book a tour for a group of friends.

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [bright] Lovely. How many of you are there?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [mildly exasperated] There were six of us, but two have had to drop out, so it's just four now.

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [upbeat] Four, no problem. Have you decided which tour?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [casual] Not yet. Which one is the most popular?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [enthusiastic] The Harbour tour gets a lot of bookings, but the food tour is by far the most popular. People love the tasting stops.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [amused, a little doubtful] I'm tempted, but a couple of us are fussy eaters. How long is the Harbour tour?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: About three hours, including a coffee stop.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: And where exactly is your shop?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [helpful] We're on Quay Street, right opposite the ferry terminal. Next to the fish restaurant.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [relaxed] Easy. What time does the Harbour tour leave?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [laughs] At nine thirty. We used to start at nine, but people kept arriving late!

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [laughs] Sounds like my friends. Are you open every day?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: Every day except Monday.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [slightly cautious] And how much is the Harbour tour?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [clear] It's forty-five pounds per person, and that includes bike and helmet hire.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [hopeful] Is there a discount for students? One of us is at university.

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [friendly] Yes, ten percent off, but she'll need to show her student card on the day.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [thinking] What should we wear?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [firmer, safety-minded] Comfortable clothes, and closed shoes. No sandals or flip-flops, for safety.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Anything to bring?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: [chatty] Sunscreen, of course. And a light jacket, because it gets windy by the water, even in summer.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [interested] We might do a second tour. What's the Night tour like?

script.speaker: Kate

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: How long does it take?

script.speaker: Kate
script.text: About two hours.

script.text: Can I book both tours online?

script.speaker: Kate

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [quiet museum hall ambience, distant footsteps echoing] [warm, engaging, like greeting a guest] Welcome to Bellview Museum, and thank you for choosing our audio guide.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [conversational, a little playful] Let's start with the building itself. Many visitors assume the museum dates from the eighteen-nineties, when the neighbouring library was built, but in fact it was founded in nineteen-oh-one.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [curious, drawing the listener in] And the building wasn't designed as a museum at all. People often guess it was a bank, because of the grand columns outside, but it actually began life as a warehouse, storing goods from the nearby docks. [softer, inviting] Look up, and you can still see the original iron beams.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [informative] Today the collection fills eight galleries. There were six when the museum opened, and two more were added in the nineteen-sixties.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [enthusiastic] Our Natural History gallery is much loved, but the most visited of all is the Egyptian gallery, with its mummies and painted coffins.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [light laugh] Our newest gallery, which opened last spring, isn't about dinosaurs or space, as many children hope. [warm, proud] It tells the story of local history, from a small fishing village to the city you see today.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [practical, friendly] Before you go any further, you might like to know that the museum shop is on the ground floor, just to the left of the main entrance. The basement is used for storage only.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [relaxed] This audio tour lasts around sixty minutes, although you can pause it at any time. [helpful aside] If you only have forty-five minutes, skip galleries seven and eight.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [cautionary, but kind] Photography is welcome throughout the museum, but please switch off your flash, as bright light can damage older objects. [reassuring] You're also welcome to sit on the benches in every gallery.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [cheerful] If you have children with you, head for the Natural History gallery, where there's a hands-on area with fossils they can touch.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [clear, gently emphatic] Please note that the galleries close at five thirty, although the building itself stays open until six for the shop and café.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [informative] Our special exhibition changes regularly. It used to change once a year, but now there's a new one every three months.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [friendly] Students can get twenty-five percent off the ticket price. Just show your student card at the front desk.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [inviting, warm] When you need a break, you'll find the café on the top floor, with wonderful views over the harbour, not next to the entrance, where the old café used to be.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [lowering his voice, as if sharing a secret] The most valuable object in the collection is not, as many people think, the gold manuscript in gallery two. [short pause] It's a painting, in gallery four, by an artist who once lived in this town.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [informative, slightly amused] The Egyptian objects you'll see all come from ancient times. The furniture beside them, which some visitors mistake for Egyptian, was actually made in the nineteenth century to display them.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [helpful] We have twelve volunteer guides as well as five members of staff, so do ask a guide if you need help. The guides wear green badges.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [admiring] As you climb to the first floor, notice the staircase, which is made of local marble. The banister is wooden, but the steps are all marble.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [practical] If you're here with a school group, please meet in the education room, on the ground floor, rather than at the main entrance.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [conversational] If you prefer to visit when it's quiet, come in the morning. The busiest time is usually lunchtime, when office workers visit.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [cheerful, bright] And finally, entry is free on the first Tuesday of every month, so please tell your friends.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [warm, unhurried] Now, press number one on your device to begin the tour. Enjoy your visit.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Welcome to Bellview Museum and thank you for picking up our audio guide.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Many visitors assume the museum dates back to the 1890s when the idea was first proposed, but it didn't actually open its doors until 1901.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A major extension followed in 1925.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The building itself has an interesting past. It looks so grand that people often get it was once a bank or a school, but for most of the 19th century, it stored goods unloaded at the nearby docks.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Look up and you can still see the iron beams of the old warehouse.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: When the museum first opened, there were just six galleries, two more were added later, which gives us the eight we have today, although we hope to reach 10 within the next few years.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Our natural history rooms are much loved and the modern art gallery gets plenty of attention, but the crowds are always biggest around the mummies in the Egyptian gallery.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: There was a lot of debate about our newest gallery. The public voted for space exploration and our children's panel wanted dinosaurs, but in the end, the trustees chose to tell the story of the town itself, from fishing village to city.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Before you set off, the shop is worth a look. It used to be in the basement, but it has now moved to the ground floor beside the main entrance.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: This tour has been designed to last an hour. You could rush around the highlights in 45 minutes, but we wouldn't recommend it.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: You're welcome to take photographs and there are benches in every gallery if you need a rest.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The one thing we ask is that you switch off your flash as strong light damages older objects.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you're visiting with children, head for the natural history gallery where young visitors can touch real fossils.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The building stays open until 6:00 for the cafe and shop, but the galleries themselves close half an hour earlier.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Our special exhibition changes four times a year, so there's always something new to see.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Students receive a quarter off the normal ticket price on showing a valid card, and children under five go free.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Many visitors expect to find the cafe near the entrance, but it's actually right at the top of the building with views over the town.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: In summer, there's also a small kiosk outside.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: People often ask about our most valuable item. Our medieval manuscript is very rare, and the bronze sculpture in the hall is insured for a huge sum.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: But the single most valuable object we own is the portrait in gallery 4.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The Egyptian collection was mostly gathered by Victorian collectors in the 19th century, but the objects themselves are far older.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Nearly all of them date from ancient times.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We have around 20 volunteers, and of our paid staff, 12 work as guides.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: As you leave the entrance hall, take a look at the main staircase.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It's often mistaken for stone, but it's actually marble.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Only the hand rail is wood.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Teachers, please note that school groups shouldn't wait at the main entrance or in the cafe, but go straight to the education room.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you prefer a calm visit, avoid lunchtime and late afternoon when the coach parties arrive.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Mornings are by far the quietest time.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: And finally, entry is free on the first Tuesday of every month.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We're also open on public holidays, but full prices apply.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Enjoy the rest of your visit to Bellview Museum.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [small community hall, light murmur settling] [bright, friendly] Good evening, everyone, and welcome. [clears throat] I'm going to explain how recycling and rubbish collection work here, because the system changed in April.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [clear, organised] Let's start with what goes in which bin. Glass bottles and jars now go in the blue bin. [slightly rueful] They used to go in the green bin with paper, but mixing them caused too much breakage.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [easy, conversational] Garden waste, so grass cuttings, leaves and small branches, goes in the brown bin.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [cautionary, firm] Broken electrical items, like a kettle or a hairdryer, must not go in any bin. Please take them to the recycling centre on Mill Lane.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [sighs] Plastic bags and plastic film are the tricky ones. I'm afraid we can't recycle them at all at the moment, so they go in your general rubbish.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [upbeat] And food waste now goes in the green bin, along with paper and card, in a compostable liner. The old food caddies are no longer collected.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [practical] Now, collection days. The green bin is collected on Mondays.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [gently emphatic, making sure people notice the change] The blue bin, for glass, used to be collected on Tuesdays, but it's now collected on Wednesdays.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [informative] The brown garden-waste bin is collected on Fridays, but only between March and November.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [light laugh] People often ask about food waste. As it's in the green bin, it's collected on Mondays too.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [matter-of-fact] And the black bin, for general waste, goes out on Thursdays.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [helpful] Next, a few items you can drop off yourself. Used batteries can be left in the collection box in the supermarket car park, next to the trolleys.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [warm] Clothes and shoes in good condition should go to a charity shop. There are three on the high street.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [practical] Large furniture, such as a sofa or a bed, can be taken to the council depot. Or, for a small fee, we'll collect it from your home.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [pleased, enthusiastic] Printer cartridges are a new one. The primary school on Elm Road collects them to raise money, so please take them there.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [serious, firm] And used engine oil should never go down the drain. Take it to the petrol station on the ring road, which has a special tank.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [encouraging, warmer] Finally, I'd like to explain why all this matters. Composting garden and food waste means less rubbish is buried, so it reduces landfill.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [informative] The car-sharing scheme that many of you have joined means fewer cars on the road, which reduces emissions.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [sincere] The bring-your-own-bag scheme in local shops keeps plastic out of rivers and the sea, which helps wildlife.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [cheerful] Our can and bottle return scheme pays a small amount for every item returned, and that money goes to local schools, so it raises funds for them.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [knowing, slightly amused] And switching to energy-saving light bulbs is good for the environment, of course, but for most households the biggest benefit is simple. It saves money on electricity bills.

script.speaker: Officer
script.text: [warm, wrapping up] Thank you for listening. There are leaflets by the door if you'd like a copy of today's information.

transcript.speaker: Officer

transcript.speaker: Officer

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [light birdsong, gentle breeze] [friendly, projecting to a small group] Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Maple Ridge Nature Reserve. Please take out the map you were given at the gate. We're standing at the entrance, at the south end, and the lake is straight ahead of you.

script.text: [clear, guiding] Just inside the gate, on your left, is the picnic area. [cheerful] That's where we'll meet for lunch.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [conversational] Right beside the picnic area, still on the left of the main path, is the children's playground.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [guiding] If you follow the path to the right, along the east shore of the lake, you'll come to the boathouse. It's about halfway up the east side, and you can hire rowing boats there in summer.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [quietly, conspiratorial] Now, if you like birds, keep going past the boathouse to the north-east corner of the lake. That's where the bird hide is, among the reeds.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [gently correcting a common mistake] Some visitors think the island in the middle of the lake is a viewing platform, but it's actually a nesting site, and it's closed to the public. The viewing platform is on the west shore, halfway up, looking across the water.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [enthusiastic] At the northern tip of the lake, where the stream comes in, you'll find the waterfall. It's especially impressive after rain.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [informative] The campsite is in the forest to the north-west, beyond the end of the path. You need to book in advance to stay there.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [fond] Next to the stream, just east of the waterfall, is the old mill. It's been restored, and it's open on weekends.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [practical] If the main car park by the entrance is full, you'll be sent to the overflow car park. That's outside the south-east corner of the reserve, across the road.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [warm, with a hint of excitement] And finally, don't miss the lookout tower. It stands on the ridge in the north-east, above the bird hide, and it's the highest point in the reserve.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [brisk, moving on] Right. Now, let's head over to the Lake View Visitor Centre. On your map, it's shown as a floor plan in the corner. The entrance faces south, and the information desk is in the entrance hall.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [clear] As you walk in, the shop is immediately on your left.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [matter-of-fact] The toilets are also on the left, just past the shop.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [friendly, correcting] The café is at the back of the building, on the right, with big windows over the lake. Not on the left, as it was before the building was extended.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [informative] The lecture room is on the left, at the back, opposite the café. There are talks there most weekends.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [warm] For families, the children's activity room is immediately on your right as you come in.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [descriptive] In the middle of the building is the exhibition hall. It's divided in two. The temporary exhibition is in the front half, nearest the entrance, and at the moment it's showing wildlife photography.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [slightly proud] The permanent exhibition, on the reserve's history, is in the back half.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [reassuring] If anyone feels unwell, the first-aid room is on the right, between the children's room and the café.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [helpful] The resource room, for school groups, is right at the back, in the centre, behind the exhibition hall.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [light, friendly] And finally, the staff office. That's upstairs, but the staircase is in the far right-hand corner at the back, beside the café. Just ring the bell.

script.speaker: Ranger
script.text: [warm, energetic] Okay, that's everything. Let's walk down to the lake.

script.text: [outdoor park ambience, distant children playing] [cheerful, upbeat] Hello, and thanks for listening. I'm delighted to tell you about the brand-new play area at Riverside Park.

script.text: [clear] The play area has been designed for children aged two to twelve. Older children are welcome in the skate park next door.

script.speaker: Officer

script.speaker: Officer

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [distant machinery hum, outdoor yard] [calm, knowledgeable] Welcome to Grasslands Recycling Centre. I'm the site manager, and before we walk round, I'll explain what happens here.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Every vehicle that arrives is directed straight to the weighbridge, so we know exactly how much material comes in.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [serious, cautionary] Staff then check each load for hazardous items, such as paint, gas bottles or chemicals. These are taken to a separate, secure area.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [informative, a little proud] Household waste is sorted into twelve different categories. We used to use eight, but we've added more as recycling technology has improved.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [explaining] Metal goes to the shredder, where it's cut into small pieces before it's sold on.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [steady] Glass is separated by colour, because clear, green and brown glass are recycled separately.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [conversational] Paper and cardboard are pressed into bales and sent to a paper mill about forty miles away.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [pleased] Garden waste is turned into compost. The whole process takes about six weeks, and we sell the compost to local farmers.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [explaining] Electrical items are tested for safety. Some are repaired and resold in our shop; the rest are taken apart and recycled.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [proud] To give you an idea of scale, we handle around forty thousand tonnes of waste a year. That's up from thirty thousand five years ago.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [firm, deliberate] For your own safety, you must wear a high-visibility vest at all times near the skips. [softening] There are spares in the office if you haven't got one.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [grateful, sincere] The centre is run by both volunteers and paid staff. Without the volunteers, we simply couldn't open at weekends.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [informative] In summer, we stay open later, until eight p.m., because that's when people do their gardening.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [satisfied] Last year we introduced a barcode system, which has made sorting much faster, because every container is scanned when it's full.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [practical] If you're a resident, you'll need a permit to use the centre. It's free, and you can apply online. Vans also need a permit.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [dry, amused] You might expect the most common item to be bottles or newspapers, but actually it's furniture. [chuckles] People throw away a surprising number of sofas.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [measured] Hazardous waste, such as batteries and chemicals, is collected by a specialist company once a month.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [determined] At the moment we recycle about eighty percent of what comes in. Our target is ninety percent within three years.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [warm, encouraging] We've also started an education programme. Our team visits local schools to talk to children about reducing waste.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [wry] The busiest day by far is Saturday, so if you're coming yourself, try a weekday.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [earnest] And if you ever have a complaint, please don't phone the council. Report it directly to the site office, just inside the gate.

script.speaker: Manager
script.text: [warm, practical] Right. If you're all wearing your vests, let's go and see the weighbridge.

script.text: [encouraging] Exactly. And what advice would you give them? I'd like you to agree on two main points for the poster.

script.speaker: Amy
script.text: [with conviction] I'd say keep a daily journal. [regretful] I didn't, and writing the report now is really hard.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: [considering] Hmm. Some people say choose somewhere close to home, but I don't think that matters much. I'd say ask for feedback regularly, not just at the end.

script.speaker: Amy
script.text: [agreeing warmly] I agree with that. So, the journal and regular feedback.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [warm] Perfect. Those two will be really helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Colin, Amy, Ravi, let's talk about your placements. Amy, you were hoping to get into publishing, weren't you?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: I was, but none of the publishers had space. So, I ended up at the local paper, the Evening Post, in their newsroom.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: And Ravi, did the engineering company work out?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: No, that fell through. I was with the city council in the end, in the planning department. They worked with architects a lot, which was interesting.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: How long were you each there? Four weeks is the minimum.

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: We both did six. I could have stayed for eight, but my course started again.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Amy, what did you struggle with at first?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: I expected the deadlines to be the problem, and the software took a day or two, but what really scared me was phoning members of the public for comments.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: I'd have hated that.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Ravi, what did your days involve?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: I sat in on a couple of public meetings, and there was a traffic study going on. But most of the time, I was going through people's applications for building work to see if they met the regulations.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: And how was your supervisor?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Very busy. Sometimes I'd wait a day for a reply, and some weeks I had loads to do. But whenever she commented on my work, it was really worth having.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Amy, what do you think you got better at?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: People assume it'd be interviewing, and I did plenty of that, but the real change was learning to say things in fewer words. My editor cut everything I wrote by half.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Excellent. Now, about the reports, don't spend pages on how the organization is structured or describing your daily routine. I want to read about what you personally gained from the experience.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Ravi, did it help with your career plans?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: I'd hoped to make some contacts for a job, and I didn't really. And I still don't know which area of planning I want to specialize in. But I did find out that I'm happier in a big public organization than I would be in a small private firm.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Were there any problems?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: Money, mainly. The bus fares. It was two buses each way.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Same for me.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: The hours were fine, and the training was good, but getting there cost a fortune.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: There is a travel grant for exactly that. It's not new, it's been running for years, and it covers buses as well as trains. But the money is limited, and by the time you two asked, it had all gone. You really needed to apply much sooner.

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: Nobody told us.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Now, the deadline for the report isn't this Friday. You've got until the Friday of next week.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: And how long should it be?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Last year's limit was 2,000 words, but it's been raised to 3,000.

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: Should we put our time sheets in the appendix?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: There's no need for time sheets or a letter from your employer. Include examples of things you actually produced.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Who marks the reports?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Employers aren't involved, and we don't use an external examiner for placements. Two tutors read each one separately. There's also the placement session next term. Last year, students gave talks, but people found them rather dull, so this year, I'd like you each to make a poster.

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: When is it?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Not week one. There's too much going on then. It'll be week three.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Will employers be there?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: A few might come, but it's really aimed at students in their first year before they apply for placements. So, what advice would you give them?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: People say apply early, but honestly, the deadlines were quite generous. I'd tell them to keep a journal every day. I forgot so much.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: I agree. And I'd say ask for feedback regularly, rather than waiting until the end.

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Visiting the workplace first is nice, but it isn't essential.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: And the distance didn't really matter, so I wouldn't tell them to choose somewhere near home.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hughes
transcript.text: Good. I'll pass those two on.

script.text: [seminar room, chairs settling] [brisk, friendly] Right, Nadia, Ethan, let's divide up the work on your tourism project. Who's contacting the tour operators?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [dry] The government reports are very long. Who's reading them?

script.text: [teasing] I'll do those. Ethan hates statistics.

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [laughs] True.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the maps?

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [realising, a little flustered] I said I'd do them, but I'm doing the reports now... Ethan, you've used the mapping software, haven't you?

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [good-natured] I have. Okay, I'll do the maps.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the conclusion?

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [sincere] I think Nadia should write it. She's much better at summarising.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [pleased] Okay, the conclusion's mine.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [businesslike] Now, your sources. The tourism board website is kept up to date, but remember who runs it. [pointed] It's there to attract visitors, so it may be biased.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [thoughtful] So use it carefully.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [slightly regretful] The textbook from two thousand and nine was excellent in its day, but the industry's changed so much that it's really out of date now.

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [accepting] I'll only use it for background, then.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [enthusiastic] The journal article by Morrison, on the other hand, is excellent. Very useful, and very clearly written.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [doubtful] I found it hard going, actually. All that technical language.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [dry, amused] It's not technical, Nadia, it's just long. Stick with it.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [explaining] The international travel trends survey covers a hundred countries, so it's rather too general for a local study like yours.

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [agreeing] That makes sense.

script.speaker: Tutor

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [decisive] Let's not rely on those, then.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [moving on] Now, case studies. For overcrowding?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. For eco-lodges?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Local employment?

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [informative] The mountain village, Bayview. Almost half the residents work in tourism.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Transport?

script.speaker: Nadia

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And protecting wildlife?

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: [enthusiastic] The coastal town, Green Hills. Their seabird programme has been really successful.

script.text: [brisk] Last thing, the timeline. When will you finish the literature review?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Questionnaire design?

script.speaker: Ethan

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Analysis?

script.speaker: Ethan
script.text: Week eleven.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the first draft?

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: [determined, slight nervous laugh] Week twelve. It's tight, but we can do it.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [pleased] Good. That's a clear plan.

transcript.text: Nadia, Ethan, thanks for coming in. Let's divide up the jobs for the sustainable tourism project.

transcript.text: And the conclusion?

transcript.text: Now, your sources.

transcript.text: The Tourism Board website has some useful figures, but remember, the board exists to attract visitors, so it may not give you the full picture. Be careful with its claims.

transcript.text: What about the 2009 textbook?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: The industry has changed so much since then that a lot of it no longer applies.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: And the article by Morrison?

transcript.speaker: Ethan
transcript.text: The International travel trend survey?

transcript.text: It covers the whole world, so it won't tell you much about our region specifically.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: There's also a government database I found.

transcript.speaker: Tutor

transcript.text: Great.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Right, your case studies.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: For overcrowding?

transcript.text: Eco lodges?

transcript.text: Local employment?

transcript.text: The coastal town?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Transport?

transcript.speaker: Ethan
transcript.text: The island. There's only one ferry and it can't cope in summer.

transcript.speaker: Tutor

transcript.text: Now, your timeline. Get the literature review out of the way by week three.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [quiet office, faint traffic outside] [direct, supportive] So, Wei, talk me through the proposal. What's the focus?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [earnest, a little nervous] I'm looking at bee populations in urban areas, and how they compare with farmland nearby.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [probing] And your main research question?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [thoughtful] At first I wanted to look at habitat loss, but there's already a lot on that. So now it's the effect of pesticides on bees, especially the chemicals people use in their gardens.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [approving] Good, that's more original. How will you compare sites?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [explaining] I'll compare bee numbers in parks and private gardens. I considered roadside verges, but access is difficult.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [suggesting] I'd also measure flower diversity at each site, because that affects bee numbers on its own.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [slightly surprised, appreciative] That's a good point. I'll add it.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: How long will you collect data for?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [reconsidering] I was going to do six months, but I think I need a full year to see seasonal changes. So a twelve-month period.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [firm] Before any fieldwork, you'll need approval from the ethics committee, because you'll be working on private property.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [reassuring] I'm writing that application now.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: What's your main method?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [clear] Timed counts. I'll stand at each site for fifteen minutes and count the bees that land on flowers.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [curious] Anything qualitative?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [enthusiastic] Yes, I'd like to interview local beekeepers about the changes they've noticed.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [pleased, then instructive] Good. For the counts, please follow a standard survey protocol, so your results can be compared with other studies.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: I'll use the national one.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [cautionary] One risk is the weather. Rain and wind reduce bee activity a lot, so record the conditions every time.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [listing] Temperature, wind and cloud cover.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [emphatic] And keep a proper field notebook. Not just a spreadsheet at the end of the day.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [slightly sheepish] Okay.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [practical] Funding. You'll need some money for travel. Apply for a small research grant. The department has one, and the deadline's next month.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [eager] I'll do that this week.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [curious] Are you presenting anything before you finish?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [shy pride] I've been invited to present early results at a conference in spring. [relieved laugh] It's a student one, so it should be friendly.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [pleased] Excellent practice. For the literature review, focus on the last ten years. Older studies are fine for background, but most of the research you discuss should be recent.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: Ten years. Understood.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [measured, cautionary] And be careful with your conclusions. With only twenty sites, don't make claims that are too general.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [earnest] I'll be careful.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: When's the full proposal due?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: By the end of term.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: And will you do a pilot?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: Yes, in autumn, before the main study starts, to test the method.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: Do you have equipment?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [hesitant] Not really.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [helpful] The department can lend you a camera, so you can photograph bees you can't identify in the field.

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [relieved] That would help a lot.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: How will you analyse the data?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [confident] I'll use statistical software. I learned R last year.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: And how long will the final report be?

script.speaker: Wei
script.text: [thinking] About forty pages. Maybe forty-five with the appendices.

script.speaker: Supervisor
script.text: [encouraging, warm] Good. This is a strong proposal, Wei.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: So, Wei, tell me where the proposal has got to.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Hmm. Well, I started out wanting to compare bees in the countryside and in towns. But I've narrowed it down. I'm now only looking at urban areas.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Sensible. And your central question?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Climate and habitat loss are obviously important. But what I really want to find out is whether pesticides, especially the chemicals people buy for their gardens, are reducing bee numbers.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Where will you be collecting data?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'll compare parks with gardens, public green space against private.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Something else that will affect numbers is how many kinds of flower there are at each site. I'd measure flower diversity as well, or you won't be able to separate the effects.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I hadn't thought of that.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: How long will you be collecting data for?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'd thought about six months over the summer, but bees behave so differently through the year that I've gone for a 12-month period.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Because you'll be on council land, you'll need sign off from the ethics committee before you start, not just permission from the council.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: The application's half written.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: And your main method?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I considered traps, but I don't want to kill any bees. So, I'll do timed bee counts. I stand at a fixed point for 10 minutes and count every bee that lands.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Anything qualitative?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'm going to talk to local beekeepers. Some of them have been watching their hives for decades.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: For the counts, follow a standard survey protocol so that other people can compare their results with yours.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'll find out which one is most widely used.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: One big risk is the weather. On a cold or windy day, bee activity drops sharply, so record the conditions on every visit.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Temperature and wind speed then.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: And keep a detailed field notebook, not just the numbers, but anything unusual you notice.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I hadn't really thought about funding.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: The department offers a small research grant, and the deadline is coming up soon.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Will you be sharing any findings before the end?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Hmm. There's a conference in spring where I can present my early results.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: For the literature review, some students go back 30 years. Concentrate on studies from the last 10.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: One weakness I often see in early drafts is claims that are far too broad. Six sites in one city can't tell you about bees across the whole country.

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'll be careful.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: When is the full proposal due?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: Well, it was originally the end of the month, but the department has extended it to the end of term.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Are you doing a trial run?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I wanted to do a pilot in summer, but it'll have to be in autumn now.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: Have you got the equipment you need?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I've got a GPS, but nothing to record images.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: The department can lend you a camera.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: And how will you analyze the results?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: I'll use statistical software, the package we learned on my stats module.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: How long will the final report be?

transcript.speaker: Wei
transcript.text: The guidelines say 30 to 50 pages, so I'm aiming for about 40.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: That sounds like a solid plan, Wei.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [seminar room, marker on whiteboard] [energetic] Right, Leah, Josh, let's compare your two sites. Start with Cliffside Bay.

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [enthusiastic, talking quickly] Cliffside has chalk cliffs. Marsh Point has no cliffs at all, just sand dunes, so it's a good contrast.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [interested] What's the erosion rate at Cliffside?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [methodical, precise] About thirty centimetres a year. At Marsh Point it's only fifteen.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the main hazard at Cliffside?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [emphatic] Rockfalls, definitely. At Marsh Point it's flooding at high tide.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: How do you get down to the beach at Cliffside?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [clear] There's a coastal path from the car park. It's steep, but it's safe.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the nearest town?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [helpful, spelling it out] Hadleigh. That's H... A... D... L... E... I... G... H. It's about two miles away. Marsh Point is next to a village.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [brisk] Now, the logistics. How big will the groups be?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [practical] Four students in each group. We thought about five, but there isn't enough equipment.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: What equipment will you need?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [confident] A clinometer, to measure the slope angle, and a measuring tape.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Safety?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [careful] Everyone has to wear a high-visibility vest, and a helmet near the cliff.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [serious, correcting] Not near the cliff. Nobody goes within ten metres of the cliff base. So, just the vests. What about the tide?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [a little chastened, then back on track] Low tide is around eleven a.m. on the day we want, so we'll be on the beach from ten till twelve.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And how long's the journey?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: About forty-five minutes by coach.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: When does the risk assessment need to be in?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [slightly surprised] By Friday. The department changed it from Monday this year.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [advising] Before you go, check the weather with the coastguard. Not an app. They know the local conditions.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [repeating slowly, as if writing it down] The coastguard. Okay.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: How will you record the data?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [pleased] On a tablet. We're using an app the department paid for, so no paper forms this time.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Who's supervising?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [a little mischievous] Two members of staff, you and Dr Price.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [light laugh] Me and Dr Price. And the report?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: It's due within three weeks of the trip.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [serious] One important rule. You can photograph the cliffs as much as you like, but no photographs of local residents without asking them.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [sincere] Of course.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [probing] And if Cliffside is closed because of a rockfall, what's the plan?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: [prepared] We'll go to the backup site, Site B, Marsh Point.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [pleased] Good. And the coach cost per student?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [pleased] Eight pounds each. It was twelve, but the department's paying part of it.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Have you got permission to work on the beach?

script.speaker: Josh
script.text: We've written to the district council. They own the beach at Cliffside.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And when do we need to decide on the final site?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: By Monday, so we can book the coach.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: [encouraging] Great. That all sounds well organised.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: So, Leah, Josh, let's compare the two possible sites. Start with Cliffside Bay. That's site A.

transcript.speaker: Leah
transcript.text: People assume the cliffs are clay because of the color of the water, but they're actually chalk. And they're retreating fast, about 30 cm a year. Marsh Point is roughly half that.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Dr Patel, any dangers at Cliffside?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Bits of the cliff come down regularly, so rockfalls are the main concern.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: How do you get down to the beach?

transcript.speaker: Leah
transcript.text: There's no car park nearby, so you walk down a coastal path from the clifftop.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: And the nearest town?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Cliffside itself, about a mile inland. C-L-I-F-F-S-I-D-E.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Now Marsh Point.

transcript.speaker: Leah
transcript.text: Totally different. Sand dunes, no cliffs, eroding at about 15 cm a year.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Rockfalls there too?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: There are no rocks to fall. The problem there is the sea coming in. At high tide, the lower areas are underwater, so flooding is the risk.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Access?

transcript.text: Straightforward. You park in the car park and walk onto the dunes. The nearest settlement is Marsh Point Village.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Which one is your main site?

transcript.text: Marsh Point, but if the conditions are bad there, we'll fall back on Cliffside, site A.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: How will you organize the groups?

transcript.text: We originally said five per group, but four works better with the equipment.

transcript.speaker: Tutor

transcript.text: We thought about GPS units, but we don't really need them.

transcript.speaker: Leah
transcript.text: What about timing with the tide?

transcript.speaker: Josh

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: And the journey?

transcript.speaker: Leah

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: I'll need your risk assessment by Friday, not the day before the trip.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Who will you check the weather with?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: How will you record your data?

transcript.speaker: Leah
transcript.text: Paper sheets blow away, so we'll use an app on a tablet.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: There'll be two of us supervising, me and one colleague.

transcript.text: And the report has to be in within three weeks.

transcript.speaker: Leah

transcript.text: When will you make the final decision?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: We'll confirm by Monday.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. This all sounds well organized.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [seminar room, soft room tone] [thoughtful] So, your survey on remote working. How many people are you aiming for?

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: [confident, then doubtful] We said thirty, but that feels small.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [firm but friendly] It is. Aim for at least fifty. That's the minimum I'd accept for this assignment.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [easy-going] Fifty. Okay.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: What sort of questions?

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [explaining] Mostly closed questions, with tick boxes, but we'd like a few open questions at the end, so people can explain their views.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [approving] Good balance. Who are you going to ask?

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: [hesitant, worried] That's my worry. Most of our contacts work in offices, so the sample might be too narrow.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [suggesting] Then recruit through a local community group. You'll reach shop workers, carers, retired people. Not just office staff.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [brainstorming] What about offering a prize draw to get more responses?

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: [sceptical] Prize draws are complicated. What about a small voucher? A coffee voucher, maybe.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [agreeable] Yes, let's do that.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: How long will it take to complete?

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: About twenty minutes.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [firm, gently disagreeing] Too long. People give up. Keep it to ten minutes.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [slightly deflated] Ten. We'll cut some questions.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [advising] And put the personal questions, especially about income, near the end. If you ask about income first, people close the survey.

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: [realising] That makes sense.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: Have you tested it?

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [casual] Not yet. We thought we'd try it on five friends.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [probing, gently critical] Make it ten people, and not all friends. The pilot's there to find any wording that confuses people.

script.speaker: Fatima
script.text: [taking charge] Ten people. And we'll use an online survey tool rather than paper, so it's easier to collect.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: [approving, then cautionary] Good. Be careful about leading questions. Something like "Don't you agree remote working is better?" pushes people to agree.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: [embarrassed laugh] We had a few like that.

script.speaker: Leader
script.text: How will you analyse the results?

script.speaker: Fatima
