script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, faint murmur fading] [lively, clear] Good morning, everyone. Next week we're going down to the coast for your first survey, so today I'll explain the techniques you'll use, and how to stay safe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The survey will cover a stretch of shoreline about two hundred metres long, just south of the harbour wall. [wry] Last year we did three hundred metres, but that was too much for one day.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk] You'll work in groups of four. Each group will have its own section of the shore.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, explaining carefully] The main method you'll use is called a quadrat transect. You lay a line, or transect, down the shore from the top to the water, and at regular intervals you place a quadrat, a square frame, and record what's inside it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clarifying] Our quadrats are one metre square. You may see smaller ones in textbooks, half a metre, but we use the larger size so the results can be compared across groups.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic, slowing down] Before you start, you must record the height of the tide. Species change dramatically between the top and bottom of the shore, so the tide affects everything.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] You'll also measure two physical factors. Water temperature, which you measure with an ordinary thermometer, and salinity, which you measure with a refractometer. [light, knowing] Some of you used one in the lab last term.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [cautionary, serious] Now, safety. The rocks are covered in seaweed and extremely slippery, so you must wear waterproof boots. [firm] Trainers are not acceptable, however good the grip seems.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic] All your data must be recorded in pencil. Not pen. [explaining] If your notebook gets wet, ink runs and the data are lost.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [conversational, slightly amused] The best time to survey the rock pools is at low tide, obviously, when the largest area of shore is exposed. We'll arrive about an hour before it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [practical] If you find a species you can't identify, don't guess. It should be photographed, and we'll identify it together back in the lab.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [very firm, serious] One absolute rule. You must never handle protected species. Some of the anemones and starfish on this shore are protected. Record them, but don't touch them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Each group will have a GPS device, which records the exact location of each quadrat, so we can map all the results together.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [dryly amused] You'll be writing a lot, and seawater and paper don't mix, so bring a spare notebook. Several students ran out of pages last year.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clear] Fieldwork will be cancelled if there are storm warnings. Rain alone won't stop us, but storms will. Check your email the night before.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [serious] Each group must also have a fully charged phone, in case of emergencies.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [practical] If you collect any algae, put it in a sealed bag, so it doesn't dry out before we get back.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [correcting, slightly exasperated] Your written report is due two weeks after the fieldwork, not four weeks, as it says on the old handout.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [helpful] When you take photographs, always include a ruler for scale. Without one, we can't tell how big anything is.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm] And finally, if you have questions after the trip, I'll be in my office until five p.m. every day that week.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk, moving on] Right, let's look at the recording sheets.

script.text: [lecture theatre] [erudite, warm] Good morning. Today we're tracing the history of photography, from the first permanent image to the phone in your pocket.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, precise] Most historians date the first permanent photograph to eighteen twenty-six. It was made by the French inventor Nicéphore "/niˈɛps/". [cautionary aside] Some books give eighteen sixteen, but his images from that year faded almost at once, so they don't count as permanent.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective, with a hint of wonder] What's remarkable is the exposure time. Not eight minutes, as students often guess, and not days either, but roughly eight hours of sunlight.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [storytelling] His partner, Louis "/dəˈɡɛər/", developed a far more practical process, the daguerreotype. It was announced in Paris in eighteen thirty-nine. Britain and Germany soon followed with their own experiments, but the announcement was French.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, correcting a myth] The daguerreotype had a serious weakness. People assume it faded, but well-kept daguerreotypes have survived beautifully. [emphatic] The real problem was that each image was unique. There was no negative, so no copies could be made.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In England, William Henry Fox Talbot solved this with the calotype. Its exposure times were still long, but from a single paper negative you could print multiple copies.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [conversational] For decades, photographs were made on glass plates. Then, in the eighteen-eighties, flexible film replaced them, and cameras became much lighter.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging] This brings us to George Eastman. He didn't invent the lens, or discover light-sensitive chemicals. His achievement was making cameras cheap and simple enough for ordinary people to afford.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [light chuckle] His Kodak slogan summed it up: "You press the button, we do the rest." [amused] You sent the whole camera back to the factory to have the film developed.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Colour came later. The first commercially successful colour process was the autochrome, patented by the brothers Auguste and Louis "/luːˈmjɛər/" in nineteen-oh-three.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic, fascinated] Autochromes used tiny grains of potato starch, dyed red, green and blue, spread across a glass plate. The grains acted as microscopic colour filters.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful, posing a question] So why didn't everyone use it? It wasn't because of poor quality. Autochromes are beautiful. It was the combination of high cost and very long exposure times. Either one alone might not have mattered; together they kept it a specialist process.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm] The breakthrough for amateurs came in nineteen thirty-five with Kodachrome, the first colour film that ordinary people could use successfully.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Meanwhile, photojournalism was changing. Colour film made little difference at first; what transformed news photography was the arrival of smaller, portable cameras, which let reporters follow events as they happened.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clarifying] Much of that portability came from the thirty-five millimetre format. It wasn't especially cheap, and it wasn't required for colour. It became popular because it was compact and convenient.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging, a little playful] Let's jump to nineteen seventy-five, when the first digital camera was built. Not in a university, as you might expect, but in a company research laboratory, at Kodak itself, by an engineer called Steven Sasson.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [dry] Its main limitation wasn't the lens or the battery. It could only store a handful of low-resolution images, on a cassette tape.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] And smartphones? The cameras themselves have improved, but the real change is in how photographs are shared. Instantly, with anyone, anywhere.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [deliberate, building to a point] So, what's the biggest shift in the whole story? Many people would say the move from black-and-white to colour. [short pause] I'd argue it was the move from chemical to digital processes.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic] And two factors explain why digital took over so quickly. Better lenses helped a little, but the key factors were, first, falling prices for memory cards, which made storing thousands of images cheap, and second, the growth of the internet, which gave people a reason to take digital pictures: to share them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm] Let's stop there for a short break.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning. Today I want to take you through the early history of photography, from the very first permanent image right up to the digital cameras we all carry in our pockets now.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So where does it all begin? Most historians agree that the first permanent photograph was produced in 1826 by a French inventor named Nicéphore Niépce.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It's worth remembering that date carefully, because some textbooks mistakenly place it a decade earlier, around 1816, when Niépce was really only experimenting with early, unstable images that faded almost immediately.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The 1826 image, by contrast, actually survived, and you can still see it in a museum today.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, what's remarkable, and slightly hard to imagine, is just how long that first photograph took to capture. The exposure time required for it was about eight hours. Not eight minutes, and certainly not eight days, but a full working day of sunlight falling onto the plate before an image formed at all.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Building on Niépce's work, his collaborator Louis Daguerre developed a much more practical process.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The daguerreotype process was announced to the public in France in 1839, and it caused an immediate sensation across Europe.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: However, the daguerreotype did have one major drawback: each image was unique. There was no negative, so you couldn't make copies. If you wanted two portraits, you had to sit for the camera twice.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This is quite different from a common misconception, that the problem was fading. In fact, well-preserved daguerreotypes have lasted remarkably well. This limitation was addressed by the calotype process, developed by the Englishman William Henry Fox Talbot.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Unlike the daguerreotype, the calotype allowed multiple copies to be made from a single paper negative, which was a genuinely revolutionary step forward for photography as a mass medium.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Moving into the later nineteenth century, glass plates were the standard support for photographic chemicals for many decades, but in the 1880s flexible film began to replace glass plates, making cameras dramatically lighter and more portable.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And that brings us to George Eastman, a name most of you will recognise. Eastman is best known not for inventing a new chemical process, but for making cameras affordable and simple enough for ordinary people to use.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: His Kodak company turned photography from a specialist trade into a popular hobby.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In fact, the slogan for those early Kodak cameras captures this perfectly: "You press the button, we do the rest." The customer simply took the photographs, sent the whole camera back to the factory, and Kodak handled the developing and printing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now let's turn to colour. Early colour photography mainly used a process called autochrome, patented by the Lumière brothers in France in the early twentieth century.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The autochrome process is fascinating technically. It used tiny grains of dyed potato starch spread across a glass plate, which acted as microscopic colour filters when light passed through them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Despite its charm, autochrome never became hugely popular with the general public, and what limited it was really both cost and long exposure times together.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It wasn't simply one factor or the other, but the combination of the two that kept it a specialist, rather expensive process.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The real breakthrough for ordinary consumers came in 1935 with Kodachrome film, which is notable for being the first successful colour film for amateurs. Suddenly families could take colour snapshots at home, not just in a professional studio.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Photojournalism, meanwhile, grew rapidly once smaller, portable cameras appeared. Reporters could finally follow events as they unfolded, rather than setting up bulky equipment on a tripod beforehand.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Much of that portability came down to a particular film format. The 35-millimetre format became popular mainly because it was compact and convenient, allowing many exposures on a single roll of film in a camera small enough to carry anywhere.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, jumping ahead to the digital era, the first digital camera was developed in a company research lab, specifically at Kodak, by an engineer named Steven Sasson, back in 1975.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Early digital cameras, however, were mainly limited by image storage capacity. That first prototype could hold only a handful of low-resolution black-and-white images on a cassette tape.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Fast-forward to the smartphone era, and what's changed is less about the camera technology itself and more about behaviour.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Smartphone cameras mainly changed how photographs are shared, letting people post images instantly to friends and family around the world.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, to sum up, this lecture concludes: the biggest shift in photography's history has been from chemical to digital processes, a change even bigger, arguably, than the earlier move from monochrome to colour.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, I want you to note two key factors that drove this shift towards digital photography.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The first was falling memory-card prices, which made storing thousands of digital images cheap and practical, and the second was the growth of the internet, which gave people an easy, immediate way to share those digital photographs with the whole world.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Those two factors together really explain why digital overtook film so quickly. Right, let's take a short break before we look at some case studies.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture hall] [crisp, confident] Good afternoon. Wind and solar power have one big problem: they don't always produce electricity when we need it. So today we're comparing five ways of storing energy: pumped hydro, lithium-ion batteries, flywheels, compressed air and hydrogen.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining clearly] First, how each one stores energy. Pumped hydro is the oldest idea. When demand is low, water is pumped uphill to a reservoir, so the energy is stored as water at height. When it's needed, the water flows back down through turbines.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic] Flywheels store energy in a spinning wheel. Their great advantage is speed. They can release energy in milliseconds, so they respond faster than any other technology to a sudden jump in demand.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [light, conversational] Lithium-ion batteries you all know. They're in your phones, but their biggest market by far is electric vehicles.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Compressed air works by pumping air, under pressure, into a sealed space, usually an underground cavern, and releasing it through a turbine later.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [interested] And hydrogen is unusual because it can be moved. You can ship it or pipe it over long distances, which none of the others can do.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Each one has a key limitation. For pumped hydro, it's geography. You need hills or mountains, so you can't build it just anywhere.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [correcting a common assumption] For lithium-ion, cost is falling, so that's no longer the main issue. The real concern now is the supply of materials, lithium and cobalt, which are scarce and concentrated in a few countries.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Flywheels are fast, but they can only store energy for a few minutes. Short storage duration is their weakness.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [slightly regretful] Hydrogen's problem is efficiency. Converting electricity to hydrogen and back again wastes more than half the energy.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] And compressed air, like pumped hydro, depends on geography. It needs the right underground caverns, usually old salt mines.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging] Now, some real projects. The largest pumped-hydro scheme in Europe is in Norway, which has both mountains and lakes.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [careful, precise] Japan has invested heavily in hydrogen, but it imports hydrogen. The major export project, making hydrogen to sell abroad, is in Australia, using its huge solar resources.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clarifying] The best-known large battery trial is in Germany, where batteries were used to stabilise the grid as coal plants closed. Australia also has big batteries, of course, but I'm thinking of the German trial.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [admiring] In the Atacama Desert in Chile, there's a solar-plus-storage project that supplies power through the night.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] And one of the earliest flywheel research programmes was in Japan, back in the nineteen-seventies, for railway systems.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk] Finally, a quick timeline. The first commercial pumped-hydro plants appeared in the nineteen-twenties, a century ago.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The first lithium-ion battery patents came in the nineteen-seventies, although the batteries weren't sold until much later.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The first grid-scale battery storage appeared in the nineteen-nineties, using older battery chemistries.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic, impressed] Battery prices fell dramatically during the twenty-tens, by about ninety percent in ten years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [forward-looking] And large-scale green hydrogen projects are a development of the twenty-twenties, and many are still being built.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm, wrapping up] Right. Next week, we'll compare their costs in detail.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture compares five renewable energy storage technologies.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pumped hydro, lithium-ion batteries, compressed air, flywheels, and hydrogen storage. For each one, I'll explain how it stores energy, its main limitation, a project associated with it, and when the key developments happened. So listen carefully as I go through them in turn.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's begin with how each technology actually stores energy.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pumped hydro stores energy as water held at high height.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: When demand is low, water is pumped uphill into a reservoir, and it's released back down through turbines when it's needed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Flywheels store energy as a spinning mass, and because that mass can release its energy almost instantly, flywheels are the technology that responds fastest to sudden demand.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Lithium-ion batteries, you already know. They're the technology most common in electric vehicles, as well as in phones and laptops.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Compressed air storage works by pumping air into an underground cavern, often an old salt mine, and then releasing it through a turbine when electricity is needed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And hydrogen storage stands out because it can be used for long-distance transport of energy. Hydrogen can be shipped in tankers or sent through pipelines to places other technologies can't reach.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, each technology also has a significant limitation.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pumped hydro is limited by geography. You need hills or mountains and plenty of water, so it simply can't be built just anywhere.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: People sometimes raise safety concerns about lithium-ion batteries, but in my view, the real limitation is material scarcity. Lithium and cobalt are in limited supply.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Flywheels suffer from short storage duration. They're excellent for smoothing out a brief surge.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But they can only hold energy for minutes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Hydrogen's main problem is low efficiency. So much energy is lost converting electricity into hydrogen and back again.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And compressed air, suitable caverns exist in more places than you'd think, so the main problem is high cost. These plants are extremely expensive to build.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's now look at some real-world projects, one for each technology.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The largest pumped hydro plant in our case studies is in Norway, a country with thousands of mountain lakes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A major hydrogen export project is being developed in Australia, which plans to ship hydrogen to customers in Asia.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Germany ran a large-scale battery storage trial to help balance the output from its wind farms.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Chile has an ambitious solar-plus-storage desert project in the Atacama, providing power well into the evening.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And one of the earliest flywheel research programs was run in Japan, long before flywheels became commercially viable.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, let's put all of this on a timeline.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pumped hydro is an old idea, but in the national grid, we'll be modeling this term.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The first commercial pumped hydro plants opened in the 1980s.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The early lithium-ion battery patents we'll focus on, the ones that make commercial cells possible, date from the 1990s.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The first grid-scale battery storage installations then appeared in the 2000s, as utilities began experimenting with storing renewable output.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The 2010s saw a rapid fall in battery costs, which is really what made large-scale storage commercially viable at last.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And most recently, the 2020s have brought large-scale green hydrogen projects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Right, let's now compare the overall efficiency of these five technologies in a bit more detail.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture room, projector fan] [vivid, measured] Good morning. Today we're looking at a Roman public bathhouse. Please look at the first plan on your handout, the floor plan. The main entrance is on the west side.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [storytelling] Visitors came in and went straight into the changing room, which is immediately inside the entrance. They left their clothes on shelves. [dryly] Thieves were a constant problem.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [guiding] From there, the route went east through rooms that got hotter and hotter. The first room east of the changing room is the cold room.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [calm] Next, in the middle of the building, is the warm room, where the body could adjust gradually.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [slightly dramatic] And at the far eastern end is the hot room, the hottest room in the building.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clarifying, correcting an assumption] You might expect the furnace to be inside, but it was outside the building, against the east wall of the hot room, so that smoke didn't get into the baths.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [vivid] To the north of the changing room is the exercise yard, an open courtyard where people wrestled or played ball games.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [gentle] And to the south of the changing room is the garden, a quiet place to relax and talk.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [guiding] Back inside. Beside the cold room, on its north side, is the cold plunge pool. [amused] After the hot room, bathers returned here for a cold dip.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] On the south side of the warm room is the massage room, where attendants rubbed oil into bathers' skin.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [matter-of-fact] And the latrine, the communal toilet, is in the south-west corner of the building, near the entrance but separate from the bathing rooms.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging] Now turn to the second diagram, which shows a cross-section of the heating system, the hypocaust. The furnace is on the left of the diagram, and the hot room is above the centre.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [vivid] At the far left is the furnace mouth, where slaves added fuel all day.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] Hot air flowed under the floor, which was raised on short brick pillars. You can see these across the bottom of the diagram, under the floor.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [amused] On top of the pillars is the raised floor itself, which bathers walked on. It got so hot that people wore wooden sandals.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The heat then rose up inside the walls, through hollow wall tiles. On the diagram, they're in the right-hand wall.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clear] At the top right, above the wall, is the chimney, which let the smoke out.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Below the furnace, at the bottom left, is the ash pit, which had to be emptied regularly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, correcting an assumption] The fuel store isn't next to the furnace, as you might expect, because of the fire risk. It's further left, beyond the furnace, at the edge of the diagram.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Workers moved between the fuel store and the furnace along the service passage, which runs along the bottom of the diagram, underneath the fuel store.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] In the hot-room wall, just above floor level, there's a small temperature vent, which could be opened to let heat into the room or closed to reduce it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [concluding] And finally, in the floor of the hot room, near the right-hand wall, is an inspection hatch, so workers could check and clean the space below.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm] Next week, we'll look at the social life of the baths.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at the layout of a typical Roman public bath house.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: I've put the main floor plan up on the screen and I'll talk you through each labeled area from A through to J. So please follow along on your handout.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's start at the entrance on the west side of the building.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Visitors would first pass through the changing room, which is labeled A on your plan. This is where bathers removed their clothes and left them with an attendant or occasionally lost them to opportunistic thieves.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: From the changing room, bathers moved east into the cold room, marked as B, a space kept deliberately unheated.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next along the route is the warm room, labeled C, a transitional space that allowed the body to adjust gradually in temperature before entering the truly hot areas of the building.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Beyond that, at the eastern end, sits the hot room, marked D on the plan, the hottest space in the entire bath house.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That heat, of course, had to come from somewhere, and that's the furnace, labeled E, located beneath the hot room, so that its heat rose straight into the hottest space without smoke entering the bathing rooms.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Going back to the changing room, to the north of it, we find the exercise yard, marked F, an open area where bathers would exercise, wrestle, or play ball games before bathing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And to the south of the changing room is the garden, labeled G, a planted, shaded space where visitors could relax and socialize away from the heat and noise.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Back inside, close to the cold room, you'll find the cold plunge pool, marked H, a deep pool of cold water bathers would immerse themselves in as a bracing finish to their visit.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next to that is the massage room, labeled I, where bathers could be oiled and massaged by attendants, a standard part of the full bathing experience.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And finally, tucked away near the entrance for practical reasons, is the latrine, marked J on your plan, a communal toilet facility often built with quite sophisticated plumbing for its time.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now let's move to the second diagram, which shows the underfloor heating system, known as the hypocaust, that made all this hot bathing possible.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Again, I'll go through the labels A to J in order.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the start of the system is the furnace mouth, labeled A, where slaves would continually feed fuel to keep the fire burning throughout the day.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The heat and hot air generated there passed beneath the floor, which was supported on brick pillars, marked B. These held the floor above a hollow space, allowing hot air to circulate freely underneath.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Resting on top of those pillars was the raised floor itself, labeled C, which bathers actually walked on and which grew uncomfortably hot in the hot room directly above the furnace.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Heat didn't only travel under the floor. It also rose through hollow wall tiles, marked D, allowing warmth to spread up the walls and heat the room far more evenly than floor heating alone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Any smoke and excess hot air eventually had to escape, and it did so through the chimney, labeled E, which drew air up and out of the building.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer

script.text: [lecture hall] [curious, animated] Good afternoon. Today's question is one scientists have argued about for over a century: how do migrating birds find their way?

script.text: [puzzled, inviting thought] Let's start with timing. Many songbirds migrate at night, which seems strange, because it's harder to see.

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Birds that fly by day often use the sun as a compass. [posing a problem] But of course, the sun moves across the sky.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [answering, pleased] So how do they adjust? They use an internal clock, which tells them how far the sun has moved, and they correct their direction.

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] There's a third system as well. Birds can detect the Earth's magnetic field, which works even when it's cloudy.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] How they do this is still debated. The leading theory is that special proteins in the bird's eyes are sensitive to magnetism, so birds may actually see the magnetic field.

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about how birds find their way during migration, a topic that has puzzled scientists for a very long time.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And one where we're still discovering new details. Let's start with timing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Many songbirds migrate at night, which might seem surprising given the obvious risks of flying in darkness. There's actually a good reason for this.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Flying in the dark helps birds to avoid predators, many of which, like hawks, hunt by sight during daylight hours and pose far less threat once the sun has gone down.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Of course, not all migration happens at night.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In daylight, many birds use the sun as a compass, orienting their flight direction relative to its position in the sky.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But the sun moves across the sky throughout the day, so how do birds adjust for that?

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: They compensate for the sun's movement by using their internal clock, essentially recalculating their heading continuously as the hours pass.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For birds that fly at night, a different celestial cue takes over.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Birds that fly at night can learn the pattern of the stars, using the night sky much as sailors once did for navigation.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This isn't something birds are simply born knowing in full.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Experiments have shown that young birds learn to find the point around which the night sky rotates, essentially learning the position of what we'd call the pole star by watching the sky as chicks.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Beyond visual cues, there's a third major system at play.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field, giving them what's often described as a kind of internal compass that works even under cloud cover.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Exactly how this magnetic sense works is still debated.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One theory suggests proteins in the bird's eyes are involved, allowing birds to actually visualize magnetic field lines as part of what they see.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: An older theory proposed something different.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The theory about iron-rich cells in the beak is now largely doubted, as more recent research has failed to support the idea that beak tissue plays a central role in magnetic sensing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: As birds get closer to their final destination, their navigation strategy seems to shift.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Near their destination, birds rely more on visual landmarks, coastlines, rivers, and familiar terrain features to pinpoint the exact site they're heading for.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Interestingly, some seabirds may use their sense of smell over the ocean, detecting particular scent cues carried on the wind to help locate isolated islands.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, here's a fascinating point about how migratory direction develops in young birds.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The direction of a young bird's first migration is largely inherited. It isn't learned from parents or other birds, but is somehow encoded genetically.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This was demonstrated dramatically in a classic experiment.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the 1950s experiment, starlings were moved from the Netherlands to Switzerland, partway through their normal migration route to see how they would respond.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What happened next was revealing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The young starlings continued flying in their original direction, simply shifted sideways by the distance they'd been displaced, rather than correcting their course.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: As a result, many of the young birds ended up in Spain and France, well off their usual wintering grounds because they had no way of recalculating their position.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But here's the key contrast.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Adult birds were able to correct their route, adjusting their flight to still reach their normal wintering areas despite the same displacement.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This suggests that experienced birds seem to have a mental map, not just a compass. They know not only which direction to fly, but roughly where they actually are in relation to their destination.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Much of what we know today comes from modern tracking technology.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Researchers have attached tiny tracking devices to individual birds, allowing scientists to follow entire migratory journeys in real time.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This research has also revealed some troubling modern threats.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Artificial light in cities can disorient night migrating birds, drawing them off course and sometimes causing fatal collisions with buildings.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In response, some cities turn off lights in tall buildings during peak migration periods, a simple measure that has been shown to significantly reduce bird deaths.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That's a good place to pause.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next time, we'll look at how climate change is affecting migration timing.

script.text: [lecture theatre] [relaxed, witty] G'day, everyone. Today, a short history of timekeeping, from shadows on the ground to atoms in a satellite.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [conversational] The ancient Egyptians used sundials, which worked well, but had obvious problems. [chuckles] They were useless at night, and of course in cloudy weather.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] Water clocks measured time by water dripping out of a container at a steady rate. Their weakness was temperature. In cold weather, water flows more slowly, so the clock ran slow.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Hourglasses were cheap and reliable, and they were especially useful on ships, where sailors used them to calculate their speed.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [precise, correcting a common claim] The first mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the late thirteenth century. Some people say the fourteenth, but the earliest records are from the twelve-eighties.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [vivid] They were huge, and they were usually placed in church towers, where the whole town could hear the bells. They were driven by falling weights, not springs, which came later.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [dry humour] Don't imagine they were accurate. They had only an hour hand, and they could gain or lose as much as fifteen minutes a day. [laughs] So being "on time" was rather flexible.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic, enthusiastic] The real breakthrough came in sixteen fifty-six, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan "/ˈhaɪɡənz/" built the first pendulum clock. Suddenly clocks were accurate to about a minute a day.

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [serious, then admiring] That mattered, because sailors needed accurate time to work out their longitude, how far east or west they were. The solution was John Harrison's marine clock, in the eighteenth century, which let sailors calculate their longitude reliably.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] On land, meanwhile, every town set its clocks by the sun, to noon, when the sun was highest. So neighbouring towns had slightly different times.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [amused] That was fine until the railways arrived. Then it made timetables very confusing, because every station had its own time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In eighteen eighty-four, an international conference chose Greenwich, in London, as the prime meridian. Paris had also been a candidate. The result was a system of twenty-four time zones, which we still use.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clear] In the twentieth century came quartz clocks. A quartz crystal vibrates at a very precise rate when electricity passes through it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [impressed] And then atomic clocks. The first practical one, built in Britain in nineteen fifty-five, used caesium atoms.

script.speaker: Lecturer

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm, relaxed] Next week, we'll look at whether we should change how we define the second.

transcript.text: The arrival of the railways made timetables very confusing because every station was working to its own local time.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To solve this, in 1884, Greenwich in London was chosen as the prime meridian, leading to a system of 24 time zones, which we still use today.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the 20th century came the quartz clock. Quartz crystals vibrate at a very precise rate when electricity passes through them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Then, in 1955, the first practical atomic clock was built, using cesium atoms, which vibrate at an extraordinarily constant frequency.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Today, atomic clocks carried by satellites are essential for GPS, and precise time also underpins the internet, mobile networks, and banking.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That brings us to the end of today's lecture. Next week, we'll look at proposals to reform how we measure the length of a second itself.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre] [energetic, precise] Good morning, everyone. Today, a short history of artificial intelligence, from its beginnings to today.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [precise, correcting a common belief] The term "artificial intelligence" was first used in nineteen fifty-six. Alan Turing had written about thinking machines six years earlier, but he didn't use that phrase.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] It was coined for a summer meeting, the Dartmouth conference, in the United States.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [conversational] Early programs in the fifties and sixties focused on logic problems, proving theorems and solving puzzles. They were impressive, but only in very limited areas.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, slightly rueful] Researchers made big promises, and when they weren't kept, funding was cut. The nineteen-seventies became known as the AI winter.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brighter] In the nineteen-eighties, interest came back with expert systems, programs designed to copy the knowledge of human specialists, such as doctors.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] These systems relied heavily on rule-based logic, thousands of if-then rules written by hand.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [dry] They worked in the lab, but in the real world they were expensive and fragile. So a second decline in funding followed, caused mainly by unmet expectations, not by any lack of computing power.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging] From the nineteen-nineties, a different approach took over: machine learning, where computers learn patterns from data instead of following rules.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic] In nineteen ninety-seven, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. It was huge news.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In the two-thousands, big data became crucial. The internet produced enormous amounts of information for systems to learn from.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [amused] Hardware mattered too. Graphics processors, GPUs, designed for video games, turned out to be perfect for the calculations in deep learning.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaging] A turning point came in twenty twelve, at a competition called ImageNet, when a deep learning system recognised images far better than anything before.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [impressed] Then, in twenty sixteen, AlphaGo beat a top professional at the board game Go. Many experts had said that would take another ten years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [matter-of-fact] For image recognition, the standard type of network is the convolutional neural network.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Language was transformed later, by transformer models. They led to huge progress in natural language processing, including translation and text generation.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [serious] There are important concerns too. The ethical issue I want to highlight today is algorithmic bias, when systems repeat unfair patterns in their training data.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [concerned] Another issue is resources. Training the largest models involves enormous energy consumption.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] And some things are still hard. Machines are excellent at narrow tasks, but they still struggle with common-sense reasoning, the everyday knowledge humans take for granted.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] The long-term goal for some researchers is general intelligence, AI that could match humans across a wide range of tasks. No system has achieved that yet.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [practical, clarifying] For next week, please read the research paper I've uploaded to the course page. Not the textbook chapter; that's for the week after.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warm] Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today, I want to give you a brief history of artificial intelligence research.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: From its formal beginnings in the 1950s right up to the present day. Let's start right at the beginning.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The term artificial intelligence was first coined in 1956, giving a name to a field that researchers had only just begun to define.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That name emerged at a specific, now famous event, the conference where the term was first used was the Dartmouth conference, held at Dartmouth College in the United States, where a small group of researchers had gathered to discuss the possibility of machine intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In those early years, progress was actually quite promising.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Early AI programs in the 1950s and 60s focused on logic problems, using symbolic reasoning to solve puzzles and prove mathematical theorems.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That early optimism didn't last, however.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The 1970s saw a period of funding cuts, often referred to now as the AI winter, when governments and investors grew disillusioned with the field's slow progress.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Interest revived somewhat in the following decade.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A type of program popular in the 1980s was the expert system, designed to capture the specialized knowledge of human experts in a particular field, like medical diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: These systems relied heavily on rule-based logic, essentially long lists of if-then rules written by hand by knowledge engineers working with human experts.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Unfortunately, expert systems also fell short of expectations eventually, and what caused a second decline in AI funding was largely unmet expectations, as these systems proved brittle and expensive to maintain in the real world.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The field's fortunes changed again with a shift in approach.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The technique that became dominant from the 1990s onward was machine learning, where systems learn patterns from data rather than following rules written explicitly by programmers.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One dramatic public demonstration of AI's growing capability came in 1997, when IBM's Deep Blue defeated a chess champion, beating the reigning world champion Garry Kasparov in a widely publicized match.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: As we moved into the 2000s, another factor became crucial to progress.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Big data, that is, enormous quantities of digital information, became crucial for modern AI, giving machine learning systems far more material to learn from than ever before.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Alongside data, hardware mattered too.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: GPUs, originally designed for rendering video game graphics, turned out to be extremely well suited to the mathematical operations behind deep learning, and this hardware advance accelerated deep learning enormously.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A pivotal moment came in 2012 with a competition called ImageNet, in which a deep learning system dramatically out-performed previous approaches at recognizing images, convincing many skeptical researchers that deep learning was the way forward.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Public excitement grew further in 2016, when the AI system AlphaGo famously won at the ancient board game Go, defeating a top human professional in a game long considered far too complex for computers to master.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Much of the progress in image recognition around this time relied on a particular architecture.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The convolutional neural network became the standard type of neural network commonly used for images, since its structure is particularly well suited to recognizing visual patterns.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: More recently, a different architecture has transformed another area entirely.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Natural language processing saw major progress with transformer models, which now underpin most modern language-based AI systems, including translation and text generation tools.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, alongside all this technical progress, there are important concerns we need to discuss.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One ethical concern the lecturer highlights is algorithmic bias, where AI systems can unintentionally reproduce or even amplify unfair patterns present in their training data.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also a growing practical concern about sustainability.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A resource-heavy issue about large models is their energy consumption, since training the largest systems can require enormous amounts of electricity.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Despite all this progress, some challenges remain stubbornly difficult.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What's still difficult for AI systems is common-sense reasoning, the kind of everyday understanding humans take for granted, but which machines still struggle to replicate reliably.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Looking ahead, researchers often discuss a longer-term goal for the field.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The term describing AI matching general human ability is general intelligence, sometimes called artificial general intelligence, a capability no current system has fully achieved.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To finish today, I'd like you to prepare for next week's seminar.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What the lecturer recommends reading for next week is a research paper, which I'll upload to the course page this afternoon, so please make sure you've read it before we meet again.
